note: The control that r2026-11-08-profile-1080p turned out to need, because its result is backwards and the comparison it was queued for is not legitimate. That run read **13.733 ms** at 1920x1080 (sum of per-dispatch spans, WARN card before and after), against the 9.749 ms this plan has been calling the 1440p figure. 1080p should be the cheaper of the two, so something other than the pixel count is deciding it. Two reasons the numbers cannot simply be subtracted, and both have to be removed before any conclusion is drawn. (1) THEY ARE DIFFERENT BUILDS. The 1440p number is from r2026-11-03-profile, which stamped the port as it stood on 2026-11-03; the 1080p run stamps f2cd1f27 (the midcount build) - the port has taken the mid-frame dispatch, the counter work and a re-cut patch since. (2) THE 1440p RUN WAS ON A BUSY CARD. Its own report says gpu_after BUSY at 93% utilisation, which by this plan's gate rule makes it invalid as a measurement, even though r2026-11-03-profile-idle later reproduced 9.751 ms on a card that read idle. That agreement is reassuring and still not a same-build comparison. So: this run is the SAME profile on the SAME binary, and it plus the 1080p run give the only honest pair. What to read - the two totals against each other, and then the same kernel name in both tables. The 1080p run's `ffn_ptx 8640x256 e8 r3` is 1.431 ms where the 1440p run's `ffn_ptx 14720x256 e8 r3` was 0.980 ms: the same kernel, 0.59x the rows, 1.46x the time. If that survives a same-build comparison the port is not pixel-bound at all and the per-dispatch cost is what to attack; if the totals come back the other way round, the 1080p figure is an artefact of the build change and the plan's original 1.37x framing stands. Also read the `400 trivial dispatches + barriers` line, which read 0.408 ms at 1080p and 0.411 at 1440p - if that is stable across builds the timing route itself is comparable and only the kernels moved.
